title: How Gut Bacteria Control Your Mood

slides.heading: How Gut Bacteria Control Your Mood
slides.body: The surprising science of your microbiome's influence on mental health

slides.heading: You Have 38 Trillion Gut Bacteria
slides.body: Your gut is home to roughly 38 trillion microorganisms — more than the number of cells in your body. This complex community, called the gut microbiome, does far more than aid digestion.

slides.heading: The Gut-Brain Axis
slides.body: Your gut and brain are in constant two-way communication via the vagus nerve, hormones, and immune signals. Scientists call this the gut-brain axis — and it's a superhighway of information.

slides.heading: Your Gut Makes 95% of Your Serotonin
slides.body: Serotonin — the 'feel-good' neurotransmitter — is produced mostly in the gut, not the brain. Gut bacteria directly regulate how much serotonin is available, influencing mood, sleep, and appetite.

slides.heading: Stress Disrupts Your Microbiome
slides.body: Chronic stress changes which bacteria thrive in your gut. This shift can trigger inflammation and reduce production of mood-supporting chemicals, creating a vicious cycle between stress and poor mental health.

slides.heading: Gut Bacteria and Depression
slides.body: Studies find that people with depression have noticeably different gut microbiomes. When researchers transplanted gut bacteria from depressed humans into rats, the rats developed depressive behaviors — striking evidence of causality.

slides.heading: Psychobiotics: Bacteria as Medicine
slides.body: Researchers are developing 'psychobiotics' — specific probiotic strains that target mental health. Early clinical trials show certain Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains can measurably reduce anxiety and depression symptoms.

slides.heading: Diet Shapes Your Microbiome Fast
slides.body: What you eat can shift your gut bacteria composition within 24–48 hours. Diets rich in fiber, fermented foods, and diverse plant matter foster a healthier microbiome — and a more stable mood.

slides.heading: Antibiotics Have a Mental Health Cost
slides.body: Antibiotics wipe out harmful and beneficial bacteria alike. Some studies link heavy antibiotic use to increased rates of depression and anxiety — a reminder to use them only when truly necessary.

slides.heading: Feed Your Mind From the Inside
slides.body: Your gut is your second brain. Eating more plants, fermented foods, and managing stress aren't just good for digestion — they're evidence-based tools for protecting your mental health.
